title: What Geometry Must Manipulation Make Operational?
notes: Open the lecture by making the title a genuine question rather than a slogan. Manipulation is not introduced as a catalog of hardware. It is introduced as the problem of turning motions, frames, contacts, forces, and task descriptions into objects that can be computed with and checked.

title: Every Visible Machine Feature Asks For A Coordinate Model
notes: Use this slide to convert intuition into vocabulary. A student may recognize the arm, but the course needs the frame on the base, the joint variable, the end-effector frame, and contact information. The important move is from visual familiarity to operational representation.

title: Robotics History Is A Sequence Of Modeling Demands
notes: Do not treat the timeline as a museum panel. Each historical shift exposes a new mathematical burden. The arrival of programmable motion changes geometry from descriptive measurement into a specification language, while dexterity and mobility expose constraints that simple point-to-point motion cannot explain.

title: Commanding A Robot Means Encoding A Motion Specification
notes: This is the first place to emphasize programmability as a mathematical event. Once a machine follows a command, the command has to be represented in a frame, converted to joint or actuator coordinates, and checked against the actual motion. That is why geometry becomes operational.

title: An Open Chain Trades Joint Coordinates For Task Coordinates
notes: Keep the map q to g(q) at the center of the discussion. Students should see that a manipulator is not just a shape but a function from joint variables to a rigid motion. Workspace and accuracy are consequences of that function, not separate vocabulary lists.

title: Machine Families Are Different Geometric Commitments
notes: Use the taxonomy to prevent the course from narrowing too early to one industrial arm picture. The chapter introduces a family of geometric problems. Serial, parallel, hand, and mobile systems share the need for frames and constraints, but they stress different pieces of the mathematical toolkit.

title: Six Parameters Describe A Free Rigid Body, Not Every Robot Capability
notes: Frame six degrees of freedom as a useful promise that must be tested rather than assumed. A free rigid body has six pose coordinates, and a six-joint serial chain is the standard aspiration. But local rank, limits, collisions, and contacts decide what can actually be controlled.

title: The Tool Frame Is Simple; Dexterity Begins When Contact Multiplies
notes: Contrast a single gripper with a hand because the mathematical shift is not cosmetic. A tool frame can often be modeled as one pose objective. A hand introduces several contact frames, object equilibrium, friction cones, and internal forces that do not appear in the object's net wrench.

title: Dexterity Is Local Geometry Plus Feasible Force Direction
notes: This slide previews why contact geometry deserves its own chapters later. A contact point is not only a point. It carries a normal direction, tangential directions, and a cone of feasible forces. Dexterity is the ability to assemble these local pieces into controlled object motion.

title: The Introduction Is A Directed Graph Of Future Assumptions
notes: The dependency map should be read as an instructional claim. Later chapters are allowed to reuse earlier geometry. If rigid motion is weak, product-of-exponentials formulas become syntax without meaning. If Jacobians and ranks are weak, dynamics, grasping, and control become untestable.

title: The Chapter Records Its Claims In A Small Check Payload
notes: Use this slide to model the course's computational habit. Even an introduction can make claims that are auditable: the graph has the expected size, it is acyclic, the serial-chain degree count is six, and the generated visuals are nonblank. The checks are modest but concrete.

title: Almost Every Later Topic Passes Through Rigid Motion
notes: Present rigid motion as the bottleneck idea, not merely as the next chapter title. Every time the course compares two frames, transports a velocity, composes a screw motion, or writes a contact wrench, it needs a reliable model of rigid displacement and frame convention.

title: Kinematics Turns Joint Motion Into A Product Of Rigid Motions
notes: The product-of-exponentials formula is a preview, not a derivation. Its role here is to show what the introduction is preparing students to understand. The serial arm becomes an ordered product of small geometric generators, followed by the home pose of the tool.

title: Geometry Enters Dynamics Through Velocities, Forces, And Energy
notes: Make clear that dynamics is not a departure from geometry. Velocities come from differentiating kinematics, forces and torques must be expressed in frames, and control closes a loop around geometric error. The dependency graph is therefore a mathematical prerequisite graph, not merely a reading order.

title: Some Constraints Govern Velocities Without Becoming Position Equations
notes: This preview helps students understand why nonholonomic systems belong in a manipulation text. A wheel cannot usually move sideways at an instant, but sequences of allowed motions can change position in surprising ways. The future mathematics studies velocity constraints and the motion they generate.

title: The Lab Asks Students To Audit A New Robotics Project
notes: Position the lab as a transfer exercise. Students are not asked to memorize the particular graph in the notebook. They are asked to build a dependency graph for a new project and defend each arrow: what mathematics must be learned before a claimed robotics capability is credible?

title: What Geometry Must Manipulation Make Operational?
notes: Close by answering the opening question with four nouns: frames, maps, constraints, and checks. The chapter has not yet developed the full algebra, but it has identified what the algebra must do. It must connect hardware examples to computable geometric objects without hiding the assumptions.
